title: `RateLimitingMiddleware never disposes its PartitionedRateLimiter; the limiter's timer loop keeps the whole host reachable after shutdown`
body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

`RateLimitingMiddleware` creates its endpoint limiter in the constructor
(`_endpointLimiter = CreateEndpointLimiter()`, a `DefaultPartitionedRateLimiter`
from `PartitionedRateLimiter.Create`) and nothing ever disposes it: the
middleware implements no `IDisposable`/`IAsyncDisposable` and registers no
`ApplicationStopping`/`ApplicationStopped` callback. `RateLimiterOptions.GlobalLimiter`
is likewise never disposed, though that one is arguably user-owned.

`DefaultPartitionedRateLimiter` runs a `RunTimer` loop (`TimerAwaitable`,
100 ms period) that only ends on `Dispose()`. The timer is rooted by the
process-wide `TimerQueue`; the loop's async state machine holds the limiter;
the limiter's partitioner delegate captures the middleware; the middleware's
`_next` reaches `EndpointMiddleware` → `RouteOptions.EndpointDataSources` →
`RouteGroupBuilder` → `WebApplication` → `Host` → the root `ServiceProvider`
and every singleton in it.

Result: after `StopAsync()` + `DisposeAsync()` a host that ever built a
request pipeline containing `UseRateLimiter()` is never garbage-collected.
In production this is one host for the process lifetime and invisible. In a
test suite using `WebApplicationFactory<T>` it is one leaked host per test
class, forever. In our suite (~400 hosts per run, ~100 MB each because each
host parses a set of XML data dictionaries) the test process grew to 22 GB
locally and exhausted a 16 GB CI runner, which surfaced as SQL Server error
596 in a sidecar container rather than as anything pointing at the limiter.

`gcroot` of the disposed `Host` in a one-host dump, all three roots identical:

```
System.Threading.TimerQueue (static)
-> System.Threading.TimerQueueTimer
-> System.Threading.RateLimiting.TimerAwaitable
-> AsyncStateMachineBox<DefaultPartitionedRateLimiter<HttpContext,DefaultKeyType>.RunTimer>
-> DefaultPartitionedRateLimiter<HttpContext,DefaultKeyType>
-> Func<HttpContext,RateLimitPartition<DefaultKeyType>>
-> Microsoft.AspNetCore.RateLimiting.RateLimitingMiddleware
-> Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.RequestDelegate
-> Microsoft.AspNetCore.Routing.EndpointMiddleware
-> Microsoft.AspNetCore.Routing.RouteOptions
-> ObservableCollection<EndpointDataSource>
-> RouteGroupBuilder+GroupEndpointDataSource
-> Microsoft.AspNetCore.Routing.RouteGroupBuilder
-> Microsoft.AspNetCore.Builder.WebApplication
-> Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting.Internal.Host
```

Disposing `_endpointLimiter` via reflection on `ApplicationStopped` makes the
same host collectable within a second, so the limiter is the only thing
holding it.

### Expected Behavior

A `WebApplication` that used `UseRateLimiter()` becomes collectable after
`StopAsync()` and `DisposeAsync()`, like one that did not. Concretely: the
middleware disposes the limiters it created when the application stops (for
example by taking `IHostApplicationLifetime` and registering on
`ApplicationStopped`, or by the hosting layer disposing middleware that
implement `IDisposable`).

### Steps To Reproduce

Console app, `net10.0`, `Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web`, one package reference
(`Microsoft.AspNetCore.TestHost`). Two files, public gist:
<https://gist.github.com/chris-fixportal/a36174da57a31565c647879f74f23d5d>.
The core:

```csharp
static async Task<WeakReference> BuildServeStopAsync(bool useRateLimiter)
{
    var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder();
    builder.WebHost.UseTestServer();
    builder.Logging.ClearProviders();
    builder.Services.AddRateLimiter(_ => { });
    var app = builder.Build();
    if (useRateLimiter) app.UseRateLimiter();
    app.MapGet("/", () => "ok");

    await app.StartAsync();
    using (var client = app.GetTestClient())
        (await client.GetAsync("/")).EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
    var weak = new WeakReference(app.Services);
    await app.StopAsync();
    await app.DisposeAsync();
    return weak;
}
// then: GC.Collect(); GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers(); up to 20 times, 100 ms apart
```

Output on Windows 11, .NET SDK 10 / shared framework 10.0.12, Release:

```
without UseRateLimiter: host collectable: True
with UseRateLimiter:    host collectable: False
```

### Exceptions (if any)

None. The failure mode is silent growth; in CI it appeared as an unrelated
process being starved of memory.

### .NET Version

10.0.12 (`Microsoft.AspNetCore.App` 10.0.12). `main` at the time of writing has the same constructor-created limiter and no disposal path.

### Anything else?

- ASP.NET Core version: 10.0.12 (`Microsoft.AspNetCore.App`)
- IDE: none; CLI (`dotnet run -c Release`)
- Repro gist: https://gist.github.com/chris-fixportal/a36174da57a31565c647879f74f23d5d
- `dotnet --info` (trimmed to the relevant lines):

  ```
  .NET SDK:
   Version:           10.0.401
   Commit:            e34a38d2ae
   Workload version:  10.0.400-manifests.b0700452
   MSBuild version:   18.9.11+e34a38d2a
  Runtime Environment:
   OS Name:     Windows
   OS Version:  10.0.26200
   OS Platform: Windows
   RID:         win-x64
  Host:
    Version:      10.0.12
    Commit:       95017c711e
  .NET runtimes installed:
    Microsoft.AspNetCore.App 10.0.12
    Microsoft.NETCore.App 10.0.12
  ```

- Workaround we ship in tests: an `IStartupFilter` that captures the built
  pipeline, walks it to `RateLimitingMiddleware` by reflection and disposes
  `_endpointLimiter`/`_globalLimiter` on `ApplicationStopped`. Fragile by
  construction (private field names, `AuthorizationMiddlewareInternal`
  hiding `_next` on its base class), which is why a framework fix is the
  right home.
- Skipping `UseRateLimiter()` in tests is not a workaround: `EndpointMiddleware`
  throws for any endpoint carrying `RequireRateLimiting` metadata when the
  middleware is absent.
- Related but distinct: `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing`'s `HostingListener`
  AsyncLocal is captured by every timer started from `Program.Main`, which adds
  a second path to the same host; clearing it alone does not release the host
  because the pipeline path above remains.

title: Improve guidance for project and npm workspace relocations
body:
## Summary

Update repository guidance so structural project and JavaScript workspace relocations have an explicit, reliable validation checklist.

The JSInterop relocation in #69052 exposed three gaps in the current instructions:

1. `docs/ReferenceResolution.md` says to run `eng/scripts/GenerateProjectList.ps1` when **adding** projects, but moving a project also changes generated project ordering and metadata. The omission caused CodeCheck failures in `eng/ProjectReferences.props`, `eng/SharedFramework.Local.props`, `eng/ShippingAssemblies.props`, and `eng/TrimmableProjects.props`.
2. There is no focused guidance for moving an npm workspace. A newer local npm accepted a `package-lock.json` that CI's npm rejected after optional `encoding`/`iconv-lite` entries were removed. The relevant workspace, lockfile, and `eng/Npm.Workspace.nodeproj` outputs must be validated together using a CI-compatible npm version.
3. `src/Components/AGENTS.md` clearly defines the sample-to-E2E workflow for behavioral features and fixes, but does not explicitly describe the validation expected for pure structural relocations with no intended runtime behavior change.

## Proposed changes

### Project relocations

Add guidance to `.github/instructions/build.instructions.md` and/or `docs/ReferenceResolution.md` requiring the following when adding, moving, or removing a project:

- Run `eng/scripts/GenerateProjectList.ps1` or `build.cmd /t:GenerateProjectList`.
- Run generation a second time and confirm it produces no further changes.
- Update `AspNetCore.slnx` and every referencing `*.slnf`.
- Search tracked files for the old project path.
- Validate that every project referenced by a solution filter exists in `AspNetCore.slnx`.

### npm workspace relocations

Add Components/build guidance requiring the following when moving a JavaScript workspace:

- Update the root `package.json` workspace path.
- Regenerate and validate `package-lock.json` without removing unrelated transitive or optional entries.
- Update tracked outputs in `eng/Npm.Workspace.nodeproj`.
- Run `npm ci` with the npm version used or supported by CI, not only the developer machine's newer npm version.
- Build and dry-run pack any shipping npm package produced from the workspace.

### Structural Components changes

Clarify in `src/Components/AGENTS.md` that pure source/project/package relocations do not require adding a sample scenario or new E2E coverage when behavior is intentionally unchanged. Instead, require validation of the affected existing tests, package outputs, direct source-consumption path, generated metadata, and build entry points.

## Acceptance criteria

- Project moves are explicitly covered alongside project additions and removals.
- npm workspace moves have a documented lockfile and package-output checklist.
- Components structural-only changes have an explicit validation path distinct from behavioral feature and bug-fix work.
- The documented checks would have detected the initial #69052 CodeCheck, stale solution-filter, and npm lockfile failures before CI.

title: Improve contributor guidance for fresh worktrees and fatal test-host failures
body:
## Summary

Document several repeatable setup and validation steps that are currently discoverable only after targeted Components builds or tests fail in a fresh worktree.

These additions would help contributors and coding agents distinguish environment/bootstrap failures from product failures and preserve useful diagnostics when a regression terminates the test host.

## Proposed improvements

### Repository test guidance

Add guidance for regressions whose expected failure terminates the test host:

- Run the normal repository build/test command first so the supported path is exercised.
- If the wrapper reports the process failure but does not preserve the fatal child-process output, rerun the already-built test assembly directly with the same runner and test filter.
- Redirect that output to a diagnostic artifact and record the exit code, fatal message, and relevant call-chain frames.
- Continue to use the normal repository command for green-path verification; direct runner invocation is diagnostic evidence, not a replacement for the supported build/test flow.

### Fresh Windows worktree bootstrap

Document that a targeted build can fail before compilation when generated repository imports have not been created yet.

When `artifacts\bin\GenerateFiles\Directory.Build.props` is missing, contributors should:

1. Activate the repository-local .NET environment with `. .\activate.ps1`.
2. Run `.\restore.cmd` once from the repository root.
3. Retry the original targeted command unchanged.

This should be described as a worktree bootstrap condition rather than a product-build failure.

### Components E2E prerequisite

Document the existing recovery step when the Components E2E build reports that MessagePack-CSharp source files are missing:

```powershell
git submodule update --init src\submodules\MessagePack-CSharp
```

After initialization, contributors should rerun the same dependency-aware E2E build rather than altering project references or build properties.

### Static web assets with NodeJS disabled

Document the targeted recovery for a missing `Microsoft.AspNetCore.App.Internal.Assets` `staticwebassets.build.json` when `BuildNodeJS=false`.

The assets project has `DefaultTargets="Pack"`, which can leave the build manifest absent in this configuration. Build it explicitly once per active configuration:

```powershell
. .\activate.ps1
dotnet build src\Assets\Microsoft.AspNetCore.App.Internal.Assets.csproj `
  -t:Build `
  -v:q `
  -p:UseIisNativeAssets=false `
  -p:BuildNodeJS=false
```

Use `-c Release` for Release validation, then retry the original targeted test command.

## Suggested locations

- `.github/copilot-instructions.md`: fatal test-host diagnostic guidance.
- `src/Components/AGENTS.md`: fresh-worktree bootstrap, MessagePack-CSharp E2E prerequisite, and static-web-assets recovery.

## Acceptance criteria

- Fresh-worktree targeted Components builds have a documented recovery path for missing generated repository imports.
- Components E2E builds have a documented recovery path for an uninitialized MessagePack-CSharp submodule.
- Debug and Release targeted builds document the explicit static-assets build required when NodeJS is disabled and the manifest is absent.
- Regressions that terminate the test host have a documented way to preserve fatal output without replacing the supported green-path test command.
- The guidance avoids issue-specific test names or implementation details and remains reusable across Components investigations.

title: VS "ASP.NET Core with Angular" template: weather data never renders (zoneless CD), plus broken unit-test setup
body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

I searched `dotnet/aspnetcore` for `angular zoneless`, `esproj angular`, `angular karma vitest`, and `angular weather forecast empty` and found no duplicate.

### Describe the bug

Creating a new **ASP.NET Core with Angular** project in Visual Studio produces an app whose sample page renders the table headers but **never renders any data rows**. The API works correctly; the data arrives and is never displayed.

Root cause: the generated workspace is **zoneless** (Angular 22 default — no `polyfills` entry in `angular.json`, `zone.js` is not a dependency and is not installed), but the `app.ts` that Visual Studio writes stores the HTTP result in a **plain mutable field**:

```ts
public forecasts: WeatherForecast[] = [];

this.http.get<WeatherForecast[]>('/weatherforecast').subscribe(
  (result) => { this.forecasts = result; },   // nothing triggers change detection
  (error) => { console.error(error); }
);
```

With no zone.js there is no patched XHR to trigger change detection, and a plain field assignment is not reactive, so the view is never re-rendered after the response arrives.

Secondary effect: `forecasts` is initialised to `[]`, which is truthy, so `*ngIf="forecasts"` shows the table immediately and the intended `Loading...` branch is unreachable.

### Additional defects in the same generated project

Three more, all independent of the above:

1. **`src/app/app.spec.ts` has a syntax error.** The file ends with `};` instead of `});` — the `describe(` call is never closed, so the spec cannot compile.
2. **The unit-test setup references karma, which is not installed.** `angular.json` sets `test.options.karmaConfig: "karma.conf.js"`, and a `karma.conf.js` is generated that `require`s `karma-jasmine`, `karma-chrome-launcher`, `karma-jasmine-html-reporter`, `karma-coverage` and `@angular-devkit/build-angular/plugins/karma`. **None of those are in `package.json`.** The workspace is otherwise configured for vitest (`vitest` + `jsdom` in devDependencies, `tsconfig.spec.json` has `"types": ["vitest/globals"]`). Current `ng new` generates neither `karma.conf.js` nor the `karmaConfig` option.
3. **`jest-editor-support` is added to `dependencies`** (a runtime dependency, in a vitest project) rather than `devDependencies`, and unpinned as `"*"`.

Minor: `tsconfig.app.json` / `tsconfig.spec.json` carry `outDir` entries that current `ng new` no longer emits.

### These are introduced by the VS patch steps, not by the Angular CLI

I generated a clean workspace with the same CLI version and flags the template records, and diffed it against the generated project:

```
npx @angular/cli@22.1.7 new <name> --style=css --ssr=false --no-standalone --routing --skip-git --skip-install --defaults
```

The CLI output has **none** of these defects. Every one of them maps to a step the template's own `CHANGELOG.md` lists:

> - Create Angular project with ng: `ng new <name> --defaults --skip-install --skip-git --no-standalone`
> - **Update app.ts component to fetch and display weather information.**
> - **Modify app.spec.ts with updated tests.**
> - **Add `karma.conf.js` for unit tests.**
> - **Update `angular.json` to point to `karma.conf.js`.**
> - **Update package.json to add `jest-editor-support`.**

The integration layer appears to predate Angular's zoneless default and the karma-to-vitest switch.

### Expected Behavior

A newly created project should display the weather forecast rows on first run, and `npm test` should run.

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Visual Studio → Create a new project → **ASP.NET Core with Angular** → .NET 10.
2. F5 (https profile).
3. Observe: heading, description and table headers render; no data rows. `GET /weatherforecast` returns 200 with valid JSON.
4. `npm test` fails — `karma.conf.js` cannot resolve its `require`s, and `app.spec.ts` does not parse.

### Suggested fix

Make the sample state a signal, which restores reactivity without reintroducing zone.js:

```ts
public readonly forecasts = signal<WeatherForecast[] | undefined>(undefined);

this.http.get<WeatherForecast[]>('/weatherforecast').subscribe({
  next: (result) => this.forecasts.set(result),
  error: (error) => console.error(error)
});
```

with `@if (forecasts(); as forecasts) { ... @for (forecast of forecasts; track forecast.date) { ... } }` in the template. Separately, drop `karma.conf.js` and the `karmaConfig` option, fix the `app.spec.ts` paren, and move `jest-editor-support` to `devDependencies` (pinned).

I understand the template itself lives in Visual Studio rather than this repo — filing here for visibility, as with #52049. Happy to also file on Developer Community.

### Exceptions (if any)

None — no console errors. The failure is silent.

### .NET Version

10.0.400

### Anything else?

- Visual Studio 18.9.12120.119 (Community). VS 2022 17.14.37314.3 also installed; the solution is `.slnx` / `net10.0`, created by VS 18.9.
- Template pins `@angular/*` at `^22.0.0` and `@angular/cli` at `^22.0.4`; resolved installs were `@angular/core` 22.1.5 and `@angular/cli` 22.1.7.
- `dotnet new details angular` reports no template package, and `C:\Program Files\dotnet\templates\10.0.11\` contains no SPA templates, confirming this ships with VS rather than the SDK.

title: Clarify API approval as an RTM requirement
body:
`docs/APIReviewProcess.md` is ambiguous about when API review must be completed relative to implementation, pull requests, merge, and release.

The process currently says:

> When an API change/suggestion gets approved, the `api-approved` label should be added to the issue.
>
> The owner of the issue is now free to work on the implementation of the proposed API.

This can be read as making `api-approved` a prerequisite for implementation or merge. That is not the intended policy. API review is a design requirement that must be completed before the API ships at RTM; it does not prevent implementation work, opening a pull request, marking a pull request ready, or merging the implementation while review is still in progress.

The later readiness guidance already acknowledges that implementation may precede approval:

> It's fine to link this to the generated ref-assembly-code in the PR.

Please clarify the process stages and make the RTM boundary explicit.

Suggested wording:

> API review may happen before, during, or after implementation. Contributors may implement the API, open or mark a pull request ready, and merge the work before the proposal receives `api-approved`. The issue owner is responsible for ensuring that the API receives approval before it ships at RTM. If implementation changes the proposed or previously approved API shape, update the proposal and return the revised shape to API review before RTM.

The process diagram and the sentence stating that the owner is "now free to work on the implementation" should be updated consistently so they do not imply an implementation or merge gate.

### Describe the bug

When running a default .NET 11 Blazor Web App in Visual Studio and launching it in Microsoft Edge, the browser console displays the following error:

`Permissions policy violation: unload is not allowed in this document`

Investigation indicates that the error originates from Visual Studio's Browser Link integration:

`/_vs/browserLink`

rather than from the Blazor Web App itself.

The issue occurs even when Content Security Policy (CSP) is not enabled and affects all Blazor Web App render modes:

- Static SSR
- Interactive Server
- Interactive WebAssembly
- Interactive Auto

The behavior appears to be specific to Microsoft Edge and local debugging scenarios.

### Expected Behavior

A default Blazor Web App project created from the Visual Studio template should launch in Microsoft Edge without producing browser console errors.

If Browser Link is using functionality that is restricted by modern browser permissions policies, it should avoid triggering console violations during debugging.

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Create a new default Blazor Web App.
2. Select any render mode:
> - Static SSR
> - Interactive Server
> - Interactive WebAssembly
> - Interactive Auto
4. Run the application in Debug mode from Visual Studio.
5. Launch using Microsoft Edge.
6. Open browser Developer Tools.
7. Observe the Console tab.

The console reports: `Permissions policy violation: unload is not allowed in this document`

**Additional Observations**

1. Reproducible with CSP disabled.
2. Reproducible across all Blazor render modes.
3. Appears to originate from localhost:<port>/_vs/browserLink.
4. Not observed when running the published application.

- Microsoft Edge
